common_name: Gold Fountains Sedge (Kaga Nishiki Variegated Japanese Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kaga Nishiki holds its brightest gold margins with a little morning sun but tolerates deep shade better than most variegated sedges.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where the narrow, arching blades keep their crisp gold margins best out of hot afternoon sun. Kaga Nishiki, also sold as Gold Fountains, forms a dense, symmetrical, fountain-shaped clump of slender bright green leaves edged in a clean golden band, a finer and more refined texture than the broader-bladed Carex morrowii cultivars already in wide use. The insignificant flowers are grown for foliage effect only, and the evergreen clump provides year-round structure at the front of a shaded border or along a woodland path. Established clumps need little more than an occasional grooming of tattered old leaves in late winter and division every three to four years once the center thins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Bronze New Zealand Hair Sedge (Bronze-Leaved Comans Sedge)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; good drainage through winter is essential, as this sedge resents cold, soggy soil more than cold air temperatures.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where winter water can drain away quickly. Bronze Form forms a cascading, fountain-like mound of narrow, hair-fine, reddish-bronze foliage that reads almost metallic against green-leaved companions, distinct from the near-white Frosty Curls form of the closely related Carex albula already grown in this collection. It provides year-round color with minimal care and is well suited to container edges, rock gardens, and small-scale groundcover plantings where its cascading habit can spill over a wall or pot rim. Comb out dead blades by hand each spring rather than shearing, since cutting back hard can slow this sedge's recovery, and divide congested clumps in early summer.

common_name: Northern Exposure Amber Coral Bells (Extreme-Hardy Amber-Leaved Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; Northern Exposure was bred using cold-hardy Heuchera richardsonii parentage for extra-tough performance into zone 3.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, providing afternoon shade in hot-summer climates. Northern Exposure Amber carries clear amber-orange, rounded leaves on a dense, multi-crowned mound, part of a Terra Nova Nurseries series bred from the prairie-native Heuchera richardsonii specifically to survive brutal northern winters where many heuchera cultivars fail. The series is also notable for strong rust resistance and foliage that holds its color and good looks later into the season than most coral bells. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring, replanting slightly deeper as the crown naturally rises above the soil line over time.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Northern Exposure Lime Coral Bells (Extreme-Hardy Lime-Green Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; lime-green color holds best out of intense afternoon sun, which can bleach the foliage.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, sheltering plants from the hottest midday sun to keep the foliage from washing out. Northern Exposure Lime is a medium-large, long-lived landscape selection with round, consistently lime-green leaves that hold their color all season rather than shifting toward chartreuse or green as many gold- and lime-toned heucheras do, forming a dense, rounded mound with multiple vigorous crowns. Like its Northern Exposure series siblings it was bred from cold-hardy Heuchera richardsonii stock, giving it reliable survival in far colder winters than typical hybrid coral bells. Established clumps benefit from division every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Northern Exposure Purple Coral Bells (Extreme-Hardy Silver-Purple Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, where the round leaves develop their fullest silver-over-purple sheen. Northern Exposure Purple forms a good, quick-filling crown of purple-to-silver foliage on a compact mound, bred as part of Terra Nova's cold-hardy series using native prairie Heuchera richardsonii to withstand winters well beyond the range of most hybrid coral bells. Airy stems of small flowers rise well above the foliage in late spring into summer, and the series is prized for holding attractive color and habit later into the season than older heuchera cultivars. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Northern Exposure Black Coral Bells (Extreme-Hardy Chocolate-Black Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; darkest color develops with a few hours of direct sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Northern Exposure Black produces ruffled, chocolate-black leaves with garnet-red undersides on a medium-to-large multi-crowned mound, the darkest-foliaged member of Terra Nova's cold-hardy Northern Exposure series bred from prairie-native Heuchera richardsonii. That parentage gives it reliable survival into zone 3, well beyond the range most black-leaved coral bells can tolerate, along with strong rust resistance and season-long good looks. Site it near lighter-foliaged companions such as Northern Exposure Amber or Lime for maximum contrast, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Northern Exposure Red Coral Bells (Extreme-Hardy Brick-Red Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Northern Exposure Red carries crinkled, round leaves that stay a clear, dark brick red through the whole growing season rather than fading, forming a dense, medium-size mound on a plant bred from cold-hardy Heuchera richardsonii for reliable performance where winters are too severe for most hybrid coral bells. The series shows strong resistance to rust, a common heuchera foliage disease, and keeps its color and form later into fall than older cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous, well-shaped mounds.

common_name: Northern Exposure Sienna Coral Bells (Extreme-Hardy Caramel-Orange Heuchera)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; foliage shifts from apple-green in spring to caramel-orange as temperatures warm.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun, where the foliage shows its strongest seasonal color transition. Northern Exposure Sienna opens apple-green in spring and shifts to caramelized orange edged in gold by midseason, a distinct color progression among the Northern Exposure series and the wider Terra Nova heuchera lineup. Bred from cold-hardy prairie Heuchera richardsonii, it tolerates a wide range of light, poor soil, heat, cold, humidity, and drought better than typical hybrid coral bells, with the whole series marketed as essentially foolproof for northern gardens. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to keep the planting vigorous and well shaped.

common_name: Happy Trails Foamflower (Trailing Black-Veined Tiarella Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Happy Trails spreads by long, wiry runners rather than staying clumping, so allow ample room or use it intentionally as a running groundcover.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Happy Trails is a Terra Nova trailing foamflower selection with small, rounded, lobed leaves marked by a thick black band tracing the veins, sent out along abundant running stolons that root as they spread, making it far more of a true groundcover than clump-forming Tiarella cultivars such as Sugar and Spice or Spring Symphony. Wands of small white flowers rise just above the foliage in spring. It works well cascading over a woodland slope, tumbling from a raised bed edge, or filling a shaded container or hanging basket where its trailing habit can be shown off.

common_name: Appalachian Trail Foamflower (Trailing Burgundy-Veined Tiarella Groundcover)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this cultivar spreads by running stolons and fills in as a groundcover rather than staying in a tight clump.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Appalachian Trail is a vigorous, mat-forming Terra Nova foamflower with heart-shaped, fresh-green leaves splashed with deep burgundy along the veins in a bold, splattered pattern more heavily marked than the fine black veining of its sister selection Happy Trails. Short wands of white flowers appear above the foliage in mid to late spring, and the plant spreads steadily by trailing stolons to knit together as a dense groundcover in shady, moisture-retentive sites. It pairs well underneath ferns and hostas along a shaded slope or woodland path where its running habit can be allowed to fill in freely.

common_name: Peach Tea Foamy Bells (Peachy-Red Heucherella with Crimson Veins)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; foliage opens red in spring and shifts to peach with crimson veining as it matures.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade, giving some protection from the hottest afternoon sun to preserve the peach coloring. Peach Tea forms a vigorous, compact mound of crinkled, lobed leaves that emerge red in spring, mature to peach with orange tinges and distinctive crimson veins through summer, then turn gold in fall, a warmer color range than most heucherella cultivars in this collection. Dainty spikes of creamy white bell-shaped flowers rise well above the foliage from late spring into early summer. As a cross between Heuchera and Tiarella, it combines Heuchera's tidier clumping habit with Tiarella's toughness in shade, and benefits from division every three to four years to keep the crown vigorous.

common_name: Plum Cascade Foamy Bells (First Trailing Purple-Silver Heucherella)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Plum Cascade trails and spreads more than clump-forming heucherella cultivars, so allow extra room or let it cascade over an edge.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Plum Cascade was Terra Nova's first purple-leaved trailing heucherella, forming a showy, spreading mound of deeply lobed, plum-purple foliage with a light silver sheen, distinct from the more common gold- and copper-toned trailing selections such as Buttered Rum or Redstone Falls. Small, light pink flowers appear on short stems from May through October, a notably long bloom season for the genus. Its vigorous trailing habit makes it useful as a groundcover in shaded beds, spilling over the edge of a raised bed or container, or massed as a color echo beneath dark-leaved companions like black mondo grass.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; Samantha stays in a tight, non-spreading clump rather than creeping like Liriope spicata.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun. Samantha is an unusual pink-flowering lilyturf selection, sending up conical spikes of soft pale pink blooms, darker in bud and lightening as they open, above narrow, arching, deep green leaves, a distinct break from the violet-blue or white flower spikes of Big Blue and Silvery Sunproof already common in cultivation. It stays in a tidy, clumping habit that does not spread by rhizomes, making it well suited for edging paths, lawn-replacement plantings between stepping stones, or containers. Trim the whole clump back to a few inches above ground each late winter to remove tattered old foliage before fresh spring growth begins.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
